title: Ashtavakra, bent in eight places
hookLine: a king asks three questions in one breath, and a sage answers without offering him a single thing to do
carry: you are the witness, free right now
tomorrow: Free if you take yourself as free

lines: A BOY WHO CORRECTED HIS FATHER.
A SAGE AND A KING, ALONE.
cards: Before the book, there's a boy, and the Mahabharata tells his story. Still in his mother's womb, it says, he heard his father reciting the sacred texts and spoke up to correct him.
The father, stung, cursed the child, and he was born bent in eight places. So he was called Ashtavakra, eight bends.

Later, still young, he walked into the court of King Janaka of Videha and out-argued the court's champion in debate. The book named for him, the Ashtavakra Gita, puts the sage and the king in a quieter room, alone.
And the king opens with a question.

teach.b: Janaka's first words, in paraphrase, are three questions in one breath. How is knowledge gained? How does freedom come?
How is detachment reached? It's a busy man asking for a method. Ashtavakra's first answer sounds like ethics.
If you want freedom, my child, leave the objects of the senses as you'd leave poison, and drink forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth like nectar. Then he turns sharply.

teach.h: NOT EARTH, WATER, FIRE, AIR OR SPACE.
teach.b: You aren't earth, or water, or fire, or air, or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these, consciousness itself.

Advaita's word for it is sakshi, the witness. A verse later comes the turn that gives the book its edge. If you set the body aside and simply rest in awareness, you are happy, at peace and free of bondage, right now.
Not after the practices. Not at the end of the road. Now.
That's how the Ashtavakra Gita reads. It hardly gives instructions; it keeps pointing at what the king already is. And notice who's asking.
Janaka is a working king, and in the Bhagavad Gita Krishna names him as one who reached perfection through action.

teach.h: A KING WHO DIDN'T LEAVE THE PALACE.
teach.b: Hindus remember him as the free householder: he didn't have to leave the palace.
Some readers find the book too abrupt to use. Others find the abruptness is the whole gift. It doesn't ask Janaka to become something new, only to stop overlooking what's already here.

how: The Ashtavakra Gita is read and studied by students of Advaita Vedanta, often slowly with a teacher, and some recite or chant its Sanskrit verses; it is a dialogue in which King Janaka asks and the sage Ashtavakra answers.

o: the court champion a boy beat in a debate
the sage born bent in eight places, Janaka's teacher
the king of Videha who asked how freedom comes

games.q: the sage and the king — tap the pairs.
p: the sage, born bent in eight places
the king who asks how to be free
how to treat the objects of the senses

s: the Ashtavakra Gita opens with the sage giving a long list of practices
it opens with Janaka's questions, and the sage points him to rest in awareness now.
the Mahabharata tells how Ashtavakra was cursed by his own father
the boy corrected his father's recitation from the womb, and the father cursed him.
Ashtavakra tells Janaka he is earth, water, fire, air and space
he says the opposite: you are none of these, but the witness of them all.

games.q: you're Ashtavakra. a king asks how to gain knowledge, freedom and detachment. what do you give him?
o: a program of practices, in order.
a reminder that he is the witness, free now.
a test he must pass first.
games.why: after a line on poison and nectar, the sage says that resting in awareness he is happy, at peace and free, right now.

practice: Notice the body, its weight and warmth, then the sounds in the room and the thoughts drifting through. Then, gently, notice the noticing itself, the awareness in which all of them show up.
Nothing to push away; just rest there, as the one who sees.

wordCard.voice: Ashtavakra, the sage born bent in eight places, who taught King Janaka that freedom is something to notice, not earn.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: Ashtavakra, the sage's name, which the Mahabharata ties to a body bent in eight places.

carryVoice: Your line: you are the witness, free right now. Six days with this short book begin here. Day nine hundred ninety-nine, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, the story of Ashtavakra
